516:     /// Open the machine-local development store. Only the `celld dev`
517:     /// supervisor and its child node receive this constructor; fleet flags
518:     /// continue to resolve exclusively through the cloud backend parser.
519:     pub(crate) fn open_dev(database: &std::path::Path) -> anyhow::Result<Bucket> {
520:         let store = Arc::new(crate::local_store::LocalStore::open(database)?);
521:         Ok(Bucket {
522:             store: store.clone(),
523:             paginated: store.clone(),
524:             cas_store: store,
525:             backend: StorageBackend::Local,
526:             name: database.display().to_string(),
527:             prefix: String::new(),
528:         })
529:     }
530: 
531:     /// The body of [`Self::open`], taking the cloud configuration instead
532:     /// of deriving it from the `GOOGLE_*` and `AZURE_*` environments. A
533:     /// caller that passes explicit sources is independent of that
534:     /// environment.
535:     #[doc(hidden)]
536:     pub fn open_with_sources(
537:         bucket: &str,
538:         endpoint: Option<&str>,
539:         region: &str,
540:         credentials: Option<StaticCredentials>,
541:         app: Option<&str>,
542:         sources: CloudSources,
543:     ) -> anyhow::Result<Bucket> {
544:         let CloudSources {
545:             gcs: gcs_builder,
546:             azure: azure_env,
547:         } = sources;
548:         let (backend, bucket, prefix) = split_spec(bucket);
549:         // The prefix is spliced into keys as plain text and stripped off
550:         // listed keys the same way. A character `object_store` would
551:         // percent-encode would make the two disagree, so refuse it here
552:         // rather than mis-parse every listing later.
553:         let illegal = |c: char| !c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() && !"-_./".contains(c);
554:         if prefix.contains(illegal) {
555:             anyhow::bail!("bucket prefix accepts only letters, digits and -_./: {prefix:?}");
556:         }
557:         // These bounds mirror the aws-sdk TimeoutConfig they replace
558:         // (connect 3 s / attempt 15 s / operation 30 s) — a correctness
559:         // condition for the node self-fence, not tuning. The read-timeout
560:         // knob collapses into the per-request bound.
561:         let mut options = ClientOptions::new()
562:             .with_timeout(Duration::from_secs(15))
563:             .with_connect_timeout(Duration::from_secs(3))
564:             .with_allow_http(true);
565:         if let Some(app) = app {
566:             options = options.with_user_agent(
567:                 hyper::header::HeaderValue::from_str(&format!("celld app/{app}"))
568:                     .context("app user agent")?,
569:             );
570:         }
571:         let retry = RetryConfig {
572:             max_retries: 2,
573:             retry_timeout: Duration::from_secs(30),
574:             ..RetryConfig::default()
575:         };
576:         let cas_retry = RetryConfig {
577:             max_retries: 0,
578:             retry_timeout: Duration::from_secs(30),
579:             ..RetryConfig::default()
580:         };
581:         let (store, paginated, cas_store): (
582:             Arc<dyn ObjectStore>,
583:             Arc<dyn PaginatedListStore>,
584:             Arc<dyn ObjectStore>,
585:         ) = match backend {
586:             StorageBackend::S3 => {
587:                 // An endpoint can also arrive through the environment:
588:                 // `AmazonS3Builder::from_env` reads the AWS SDK's standard
589:                 // AWS_ENDPOINT_URL / AWS_ENDPOINT into the client. The
590:                 // path-style decision below must see that endpoint too —
591:                 // an env-supplied endpoint with virtual-hosted-style
592:                 // requests half-configures the client, and against an
593:                 // S3-compatible store every operation then fails with a
594:                 // NoSuchBucket that names the key prefix, pointing well
595:                 // away from the cause. An explicit argument (--endpoint /
596:                 // S3_ENDPOINT, resolved by the caller) still wins.
597:                 let endpoint = endpoint.map(str::to_string).or_else(resolve_env_endpoint);
598:                 let mut builder = AmazonS3Builder::from_env()
599:                     .with_bucket_name(bucket)
600:                     .with_region(region)
601:                     .with_conditional_put(S3ConditionalPut::ETagMatch)
602:                     .with_retry(retry)
603:                     .with_client_options(options);
604:                 if let Some(endpoint) = endpoint.as_deref() {
605:                     // Path-style against explicit S3-compatible endpoints, exactly
606:                     // as the aws client's force_path_style(endpoint.is_some()).
607:                     builder = builder
608:                         .with_endpoint(endpoint)
609:                         .with_virtual_hosted_style_request(false);
610:                 } else {
611:                     builder = builder.with_virtual_hosted_style_request(true);
612:                 }
613:                 if let Some(credentials) = credentials {
614:                     builder = builder
615:                         .with_access_key_id(credentials.access_key_id)
616:                         .with_secret_access_key(credentials.secret_access_key);
617:                     if let Some(token) = credentials.session_token {
618:                         builder = builder.with_token(token);
619:                     }
620:                 }
621:                 let cas_builder = builder.clone().with_retry(cas_retry);
622:                 let client = Arc::new(builder.build().context("build s3 client")?);
623:                 (
624:                     client.clone(),
625:                     client,
626:                     Arc::new(cas_builder.build().context("build s3 cas client")?),
627:                 )
628:             }
629:             StorageBackend::Gcs => {
630:                 // The generation dialect only. celld's S3 client fences
631:                 // with If-Match, which GCS does not apply to a PUT; and
632:                 // this GCS client authenticates with OAuth, not HMAC keys.
633:                 // So an S3 endpoint or S3 static credentials with gs:// is
634:                 // a configuration error, not something to quietly
635:                 // reinterpret.
636:                 if endpoint.is_some() {
637:                     anyhow::bail!(
638:                         "a gs:// bucket takes no S3 endpoint; unset --endpoint / S3_ENDPOINT"
639:                     );
640:                 }
641:                 if credentials.is_some() {
642:                     anyhow::bail!(
643:                         "a gs:// bucket cannot use S3 static credentials; it authenticates \
644:                          with Google Application Default Credentials"
645:                     );
646:                 }
647:                 let builder = gcs_builder
648:                     .with_bucket_name(bucket)
649:                     .with_retry(retry)
650:                     .with_client_options(options);
651:                 let cas_builder = builder.clone().with_retry(cas_retry);
652:                 let client = Arc::new(builder.build().context("build gcs client")?);
653:                 (
654:                     client.clone(),
655:                     client,
656:                     Arc::new(cas_builder.build().context("build gcs cas client")?),
657:                 )
658:             }
659:             StorageBackend::Azure => {
660:                 // The etag dialect again — Put Blob applies If-None-Match
661:                 // and If-Match — but a different client and different
662:                 // credentials. So an S3 endpoint or S3 static credentials
663:                 // with az:// is a configuration error, exactly as it is
664:                 // with gs://, and not something to quietly reinterpret.
665:                 if endpoint.is_some() {
666:                     anyhow::bail!(
667:                         "an az:// bucket takes no S3 endpoint; unset --endpoint / S3_ENDPOINT"
668:                     );
669:                 }
670:                 if credentials.is_some() {
671:                     anyhow::bail!(
672:                         "an az:// bucket cannot use S3 static credentials; it authenticates \
673:                          with an Azure storage account key, a managed identity, or a \
674:                          workload identity"
675:                     );
676:                 }
677:                 let builder = azure_builder_for(&azure_env, bucket)?
678:                     .with_retry(retry)
679:                     .with_client_options(options);
680:                 let cas_builder = builder.clone().with_retry(cas_retry);
681:                 let client = Arc::new(builder.build().context("build azure client")?);
682:                 (
683:                     client.clone(),
684:                     client,
685:                     Arc::new(cas_builder.build().context("build azure cas client")?),
686:                 )
687:             }
688:             StorageBackend::Local => {
689:                 unreachable!("the local development store has its own constructor")
690:             }
691:         };
692:         Ok(Bucket {
693:             store,
694:             paginated,
695:             cas_store,
696:             backend,
697:             name: bucket.to_string(),
698:             prefix,
699:         })
700:     }

832:     /// Conditional write. `token: None` requires the key to be absent;
833:     /// `Some` requires the current CAS token — the etag on S3 and on
834:     /// Azure Blob Storage (If-Match), the generation on GCS
835:     /// (x-goog-if-generation-match).
836:     /// `Ok(Some(new_token))` applied, `Ok(None)` cleanly rejected; any
837:     /// other failure is ambiguous and stays an error.
838:     pub async fn put_cas(
839:         &self,
840:         key: &str,
841:         body: impl Into<PutPayload>,
842:         token: Option<&str>,
843:     ) -> anyhow::Result<Option<String>> {
844:         let key = self.key(key);
845:         let mode = match token {
846:             None => PutMode::Create,
847:             Some(token) => PutMode::Update(self.backend.update(token)),
848:         };
849:         match self
850:             .cas_store
851:             .put_opts(
852:                 &Path::from(key.as_str()),
853:                 body.into(),
854:                 PutOptions::from(mode),
855:             )
856:             .await
857:         {
858:             Ok(result) => {
859:                 // The write applied; a result without a usable token still
860:                 // surfaces as `Err`, which callers already treat as "may
861:                 // have committed" and reconcile.
862:                 let token = self
863:                     .backend
864:                     .token(result.e_tag, result.version)
865:                     .with_context(|| {
866:                         format!(
867:                             "conditional write {}://{}/{key} applied without a CAS token",
868:                             self.scheme(),
869:                             self.name
870:                         )
871:                     })?;
872:                 Ok(Some(token))
873:             }
874:             Err(error) if is_clean_cas_rejection(&error) => Ok(None),
875:             Err(error) => Err(anyhow!(error).context(format!(
876:                 "conditional write {}://{}/{key} may have committed",
877:                 self.scheme(),
878:                 self.name
879:             ))),
880:         }
881:     }

896:     /// Batched delete: the S3-family backends fold this into DeleteObjects
897:     /// requests (up to 1,000 keys per class A operation) — the lab priced
898:     /// bundle GC's one-key-at-a-time deletes at 9k operations an hour.
899:     /// Returns the keys that are now gone; an absent key counts as gone,
900:     /// and a key that fails stays listed for the next pass.
901:     pub async fn delete_many(&self, keys: &[String]) -> Vec<String> {
902:         let locations = futures_util::stream::iter(
903:             keys.iter()
904:                 .map(|key| Ok(Path::from(self.key(key).as_str())))
905:                 .collect::<Vec<_>>(),
906:         )
907:         .boxed();
908:         let mut gone = Vec::with_capacity(keys.len());
909:         let mut results = self.store.delete_stream(locations);
910:         while let Some(result) = results.next().await {
911:             match result {
912:                 Ok(path) => gone.push(self.unkey(path.as_ref()).to_string()),
913:                 Err(Error::NotFound { path, .. }) => {
914:                     gone.push(self.unkey(&path).to_string());
915:                 }
916:                 Err(error) => {
917:                     tracing::warn!(%error, "batched delete left a key for the next pass");
918:                 }
919:             }
920:         }
921:         gone
922:     }

924:     /// Every object under `prefix/`; the client paginates internally.
925:     /// Listed keys come back the way the caller wrote them, because the
926:     /// caller parses them and knows nothing of the fleet's prefix.
927:     pub async fn list(&self, prefix: &str) -> anyhow::Result<Vec<ObjectMeta>> {
928:         let path = Path::from(self.key(prefix.trim_end_matches('/')));
929:         let mut stream = self.store.list(Some(&path));
930:         let mut objects = Vec::new();
931:         while let Some(meta) = stream.next().await {
932:             let mut meta =
933:                 meta.with_context(|| format!("list {}://{}/{path}", self.scheme(), self.name))?;
934:             if !self.prefix.is_empty() {
935:                 // The listing gave object_store a valid key, so re-parsing
936:                 // the tail of it cannot fail.
937:                 meta.location = Path::parse(self.unkey(meta.location.as_ref())).unwrap();
938:             }
939:             objects.push(meta);
940:         }
941:         Ok(objects)
942:     }

958:     /// One page of the immediate child "directories" under `prefix/`.
959:     ///
960:     /// `start_after` resumes from a child a previous page returned, and
961:     /// `page_token` continues the same walk. Pass one or the other: a
962:     /// token is exact and works on every backend, while `start_after`
963:     /// survives between separate processes, so an operator can resume a
964:     /// listing by name.
965:     ///
966:     /// The store compares `start_after` against object keys, not against
967:     /// children, and every key below `prefix/child/` sorts after that
968:     /// prefix itself. So the page that resumes a walk repeats the child it
969:     /// resumed from, and the caller drops it. The reverse error would skip
970:     /// a cell, so the boundary is deliberately inclusive.
971:     pub async fn common_prefixes_page(
972:         &self,
973:         prefix: &str,
974:         start_after: Option<&str>,
975:         page_token: Option<String>,
976:         max_keys: usize,
977:     ) -> anyhow::Result<CommonPrefixPage> {
978:         // `PaginatedListStore` does not append the delimiter the way
979:         // `ObjectStore::list_with_delimiter` does, so the prefix carries it.
980:         let path = self.key(&format!("{}/", prefix.trim_end_matches('/')));
981:         if start_after.is_some() && self.backend == StorageBackend::Azure {
982:             anyhow::bail!(
983:                 "az:// cannot resume a listing by name, because Azure listing has no \
984:                  start-after; drop --after and list the whole container"
985:             );
986:         }
987:         let result = self
988:             .paginated
989:             .list_paginated(
990:                 Some(path.as_str()),
991:                 PaginatedListOptions {
992:                     offset: start_after.map(|child| self.key(&format!("{child}/"))),
993:                     delimiter: Some(std::borrow::Cow::Borrowed("/")),
994:                     max_keys: Some(max_keys),
995:                     page_token,
996:                     ..PaginatedListOptions::default()
997:                 },
998:             )
999:             .await
1000:             .with_context(|| format!("list {}://{}/{path}", self.scheme(), self.name))?;
1001:         Ok(CommonPrefixPage {
1002:             prefixes: result
1003:                 .result
1004:                 .common_prefixes
1005:                 .into_iter()
1006:                 .map(|child| self.unkey(child.as_ref()).to_string())
1007:                 .collect(),
1008:             page_token: result.page_token,
1009:         })
1010:     }

1016:     /// listing. A caller that only needs a bounded answer must use

1033:     //
1034:     // An `r2_buckets` binding is served out of the fleet bucket under the
1035:     // reserved `r2/<bucket_name>/` prefix, so a Worker's blobs share the
1036:     // durability and the credentials of everything else celld stores and
1037:     // need no second bucket. These are the only operations that reach past
1038:     // the in-memory `Bytes` contract the rest of this module keeps: a blob
1039:     // is a Worker's payload and can be far larger than a fleet object, so
1040:     // it is read as a stream and a large write goes through multipart.

1054:             .await

1064:     /// One blob a `get` answered, with its body still on the wire.
1065:     pub async fn get_blob(
1066:         &self,
1067:         key: &str,
1068:         range: BlobRange,
1069:         conditions: &BlobConditions,
1070:     ) -> anyhow::Result<BlobRead> {
1071:         let scoped = self.key(key);
1072:         let options = GetOptions {
1073:             range: match range {
1074:                 BlobRange::Whole => None,
1075:                 BlobRange::From(offset) => Some(GetRange::Offset(offset)),
1076:                 BlobRange::Bounded { offset, length } => {
1077:                     Some(GetRange::Bounded(offset..offset.saturating_add(length)))
1078:                 }
1079:                 BlobRange::Suffix(length) => Some(GetRange::Suffix(length)),
1080:             },
1081:             if_match: conditions.if_match.clone(),
1082:             if_none_match: conditions.if_none_match.clone(),
1083:             ..GetOptions::default()
1084:         };
1085:         let result = match self
1086:             .store
1087:             .get_opts(&Path::from(scoped.as_str()), options)
1088:             .await
1089:         {
1090:             Ok(result) => result,
1091:             // Only an absent key is a miss. A range that overshoots the end
1092:             // of the object is served short, as R2 serves it; a range that
1093:             // *starts* past the end is a 416, and it stays an error rather
1094:             // than being turned into a miss, because that is what R2 does
1095:             // with one too.
1096:             Err(Error::NotFound { .. }) => return Ok(BlobRead::Missing),
1097:             // The store says only that the condition failed. R2 answers a
1098:             // refused `onlyIf` with the object itself, minus the body, so
1099:             // one more head fills in what the caller is entitled to see.
1100:             Err(Error::Precondition { .. } | Error::NotModified { .. }) => {
1101:                 return Ok(match self.head_blob(key).await? {
1102:                     Some(meta) => BlobRead::Unmet(meta),
1103:                     None => BlobRead::Missing,
1104:                 })
1105:             }
1106:             Err(error) => {
1107:                 return Err(anyhow!(error).context(format!(
1108:                     "read {}://{}/{scoped}",
1109:                     self.scheme(),
1110:                     self.name
1111:                 )))
1112:             }
1113:         };
1114:         let meta = self.blob_meta(&result.meta, &result.attributes);
1115:         // The upload-time half of `onlyIf` is answered here, against the
1116:         // millisecond the object carries. The body is dropped unread.
1117:         if !conditions.time_met(meta.uploaded_ms) {
1118:             return Ok(BlobRead::Unmet(meta));
1119:         }
1120:         // `range` is the slice this response actually carries, which is
1121:         // what the caller reads; a bounded request past the end is clamped
1122:         // here rather than by the store.
1123:         let served = result.range.clone();
1124:         let label = format!("read body {}://{}/{scoped}", self.scheme(), self.name);
1125:         let body = result
1126:             .into_stream()
1127:             .map(move |chunk| match chunk {
1128:                 Ok(bytes) => Ok(bytes.to_vec()),
1129:                 Err(error) => Err(format!("{label}: {error}")),
1130:             })
1131:             .boxed();
1132:         Ok(BlobRead::Hit(Blob {
1133:             meta,
1134:             range: (served.start, served.end.saturating_sub(served.start)),
1135:             body,
1136:         }))
1137:     }

1139:     /// A plain (non-multipart) write, carrying R2's `httpMetadata` and
1140:     /// `customMetadata`.
1141:     ///
1142:     /// `conditions` is R2's `onlyIf`, and is answered by reading the
1143:     /// object first and pairing the verdict with that version's CAS token:
1144:     /// the check and the write then apply to the same version, and a racing
1145:     /// write between them is refused rather than overwritten. `Ok(None)` is
1146:     /// a refused precondition — R2 reports one as a `null` return, not a
1147:     /// throw — and every other failure stays an error.
1148:     pub async fn put_blob(
1149:         &self,
1150:         key: &str,
1151:         body: PutPayload,
1152:         attributes: &BlobAttributes,
1153:         conditions: &BlobConditions,
1154:     ) -> anyhow::Result<Option<BlobMeta>> {
1155:         let size = body.content_length() as u64;
1156:         let mode = match conditions.is_empty() {
1157:             true => PutMode::Overwrite,
1158:             false => match self.head_blob(key).await? {
1159:                 Some(current) => {
1160:                     if !conditions.etag_met(current.etag.as_deref())
1161:                         || !conditions.time_met(current.uploaded_ms)
1162:                     {
1163:                         return Ok(None);
1164:                     }
1165:                     let Some(cas) = current.cas else {
1166:                         return Err(anyhow!(
1167:                             "conditional R2 write of {}://{}/{key} cannot be fenced: \
1168:                              the store answered no version token",
1169:                             self.scheme(),
1170:                             self.name
1171:                         ));
1172:                     };
1173:                     PutMode::Update(self.backend.update(&cas))
1174:                 }
1175:                 // Nothing there: only a condition that an absent object can
1176:                 // satisfy may write, and it writes as a create so that a
1177:                 // racing create loses.
1178:                 None => match conditions.etag_met(None) {
1179:                     true => PutMode::Create,
1180:                     false => return Ok(None),
1181:                 },
1182:             },
1183:         };
1184:         let conditional = !matches!(mode, PutMode::Overwrite);
1185:         let store = match conditional {
1186:             true => &self.cas_store,
1187:             false => &self.store,
1188:         };
1189:         let scoped = self.key(key);
1190:         let options = PutOptions {
1191:             mode,
1192:             attributes: attributes.write(),
1193:             ..PutOptions::default()
1194:         };
1195:         match store
1196:             .put_opts(&Path::from(scoped.as_str()), body, options)

420: /// must agree on this or identical code deploys as two versions depending on
421: /// the path used.

424: /// `Manifest::raw_metadata`; callers pass the same bytes to both.
425: /// Cron trigger expressions are deliberately NOT an input. A version names
426: /// the code and its bindings; a schedule is configuration layered on top,
427: /// which is also how Cloudflare models it — schedules are their own resource,
428: /// set by their own API call after the script upload. Hashing them would make
429: /// the native and managed paths disagree about what a version is.

432:     metadata_json: &[u8],
433:     asset_index: Option<&[u8]>,

435:     let mut sorted = modules.iter().collect::<Vec<_>>();
436:     sorted.sort_by(|left, right| left.0.cmp(&right.0));
437:     let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
438:     for (name, bytes) in sorted {
439:         hasher.update(name.as_bytes());
440:         hasher.update([0]);
441:         hasher.update(bytes);
442:     }
443:     hasher.update(metadata_json);
444:     if let Some(index) = asset_index {
445:         hasher.update([0]);
446:         hasher.update(b"assets.json");
447:         hasher.update([0]);
448:         hasher.update(index);
449:     }
450:     format!("{:x}", hasher.finalize())[..16].to_string()
451: }

1: // Copyright 2026 Deno Land Inc. Apache-2.0 license.

3: //! The input gate, reified sans-IO.
4: //!
5: //! A cell serves several requests at once — that is the Durable Object
6: //! contract, and D1 restores it by deleting the per-cell thread that
7: //! accidentally forbade it. Concurrency is only safe if a handler that
8: //! must not be interrupted cannot be, or it would resume to find its own
9: //! state changed underneath it by whatever ran while it waited.
10: //!
11: //! workerd's rule (`io-gate.h`): while the gate is held, **no incoming
12: //! event of any kind is delivered** to that cell except the event holding
13: //! it. Not just new requests — a subrequest's response, a timer, a stream
14: //! read. Anything that would run JS and observe state.
15: //!
16: //! **What holds it here is not storage.** In workerd the async KV API
17: //! (`actor-state.h:49`, `jsg::Promise<...> get`) can genuinely suspend on an
18: //! `ActorCache` miss, so storage is what gates; the SQL API (`sql.h:41`,
19: //! `exec` returning a `Cursor`) is synchronous and does not. In celld every
20: //! storage path is local SQLite underneath, including the async-shaped one,
21: //! whose `await Promise.resolve()` drains in the same microtask checkpoint.
22: //! A read or a write therefore completes inside the turn that started it and
23: //! never yields to another event, so there is no window for the gate to
24: //! close.
25: //!
26: //! Its user is **`blockConcurrencyWhile`** (`harness.js:1001`), which holds
27: //! across arbitrary user code — including real awaits like `fetch` — and
28: //! whose entire purpose is that nothing else runs meanwhile.
29: //!
30: //! # Why there is no queue here
31: //!
32: //! An earlier version of this file parked refused events in a `VecDeque` and
33: //! returned them from `release`. That mirrored a queue the shell already
34: //! owns: a cell's events arrive on its job channel, and an event the gate
35: //! refuses is simply **left there**, in arrival order, until a later
36: //! delivery attempt takes it. Modelling it twice bought nothing and cost the
37: //! two structures agreeing.
38: //!
39: //! # Why acquiring cannot fail
40: //!
41: //! [`acquire`](InputGate::acquire) panics if another event holds the gate,
42: //! and that is not optimism. Acquiring happens *during* an event, and an
43: //! event only runs because a delivery point found the gate open. So a second
44: //! event cannot be running to acquire second. Nested blocks within one event
45: //! are counted, not refused, because that event already holds it.
46: //!
47: //! This property is what makes the mechanism small, and losing it is what
48: //! wedged cells before: while acquiring was asynchronous, a cell could
49: //! deliver a second event in the window between a block starting and the
50: //! gate shutting. That event then had to *wait* for a gate held by an event
51: //! suspended beneath it on the stack, which nothing could ever release.
52: //! Acquiring is therefore synchronous with the JS call that asks for it, and
53: //! the panic is what says so.
54: //!
55: //! This is the decision half. The shell owns the delivery points and asks
56: //! [`is_open`](InputGate::is_open) at each one; it never decides who runs.
57: 
58: /// An event delivered to a cell: a request turn, an alarm, a subrequest
59: /// response, a stream wakeup. The shell assigns the ids and only needs them
60: /// to be unique among a cell's live events.
61: pub type EventId = u64;
62: 
63: /// One cell's input gate.
64: ///
65: /// Default is open, which is the common case: a cell with nothing blocking
66: /// delivers everything immediately and this costs a branch.
67: #[derive(Clone, Debug, Default, PartialEq, Eq)]
68: pub struct InputGate {
69:     /// The event holding the gate, if any.
70:     holder: Option<EventId>,
71:     /// How many holds the holder has taken at once.
72:     ///
73:     /// `blockConcurrencyWhile` nests. Opening the gate when the innermost
74:     /// block ends would admit another event while the outer ones still run,
75:     /// which a boolean would do.
76:     outstanding: u32,
77: }
78: 
79: impl InputGate {
80:     pub fn new() -> Self {
81:         Self::default()
82:     }
83: 
84:     /// May an event that is not already running be delivered now?
85:     ///
86:     /// The one question a delivery point asks. The holder never asks it: it
87:     /// is already running, and its own continuations are not deliveries.
88:     pub fn is_open(&self) -> bool {
89:         self.holder.is_none()
90:     }
91: 
92:     /// `event` entered a `blockConcurrencyWhile`. Shuts the gate, and
93:     /// answers whether it got it.
94:     ///
95:     /// `false` means another event holds it and this one must wait. That
96:     /// used to be impossible: while a cell's events came off one channel
97:     /// only one ran at a time, and a delivery point had already found the
98:     /// gate open. Events are independent tasks now, several are in flight
99:     /// at once by design, so two can reach a block together.
100:     #[must_use]
101:     pub fn acquire(&mut self, event: EventId) -> bool {
102:         match self.holder {
103:             None => {
104:                 self.holder = Some(event);
105:                 self.outstanding = 1;
106:                 true
107:             }
108:             Some(holder) if holder == event => {
109:                 self.outstanding += 1;
110:                 true
111:             }
112:             Some(_) => false,
113:         }
114:     }
115: 
116:     /// One of `event`'s blocks ended. The gate opens when the last one does.
117:     ///
118:     /// # Panics
119:     ///
120:     /// If `event` does not hold the gate. Opening a gate somebody else
121:     /// depends on is worse than stopping.
122:     pub fn release(&mut self, event: EventId) {
123:         match self.holder {
124:             Some(holder) if holder == event => {}
125:             Some(holder) => panic!("input gate held by event {holder}, released by {event}"),
126:             None => panic!("input gate released by {event} while open"),
127:         }
128:         self.outstanding -= 1;
129:         if self.outstanding == 0 {
130:             self.holder = None;
131:         }
132:     }
133: 
134:     /// The holder died — terminated, cancelled, or timed out — and will
135:     /// never release.
136:     ///
137:     /// Without this a request killed mid-block shuts its cell's gate
138:     /// forever, and the cell accepts nothing again. JS `finally` covers
139:     /// every ordinary exit, a throw included; this covers the one exit that
140:     /// runs no JS.
141:     pub fn abandon(&mut self) {
142:         self.holder = None;
143:         self.outstanding = 0;
144:     }
145: }

1: # Telemetry
2: 
3: celld can record traces and logs for the requests it serves. The
4: feature is off by default, and the off state costs nothing. Set
5: `CELLD_OTEL=1` to turn it on.
6: 
7: The default sink is the fleet bucket. celld writes Parquet files under
8: the `telemetry/` prefix, so a fleet with a bucket has observability
9: with no other service. DuckDB can query these files directly. An
10: alternative sink sends the same data to an OpenTelemetry collector.
11: 
12: The schema is version `v0-unstable`. The column names can change
13: before a stable release, and each file carries the schema version in
14: its object metadata.
15: 
16: ## Configuration
17: 
18: | variable | default | effect |
19: | --- | --- | --- |
20: | `CELLD_OTEL` | `0` | Set this value to `1` to enable telemetry. |
21: | `CELLD_OTEL_SINK` | `bucket` | `bucket` writes Parquet to the fleet bucket. `otlp` sends OTLP/HTTP protobuf to a collector instead. |
22: | `CELLD_OTEL_BUCKET` | the fleet bucket | A different bucket for the Parquet files, on the same endpoint and credentials. |
23: | `CELLD_OTEL_RETENTION` | `30d` | celld deletes telemetry files older than this. `none` disables the deletion, so your own lifecycle rules can control the data. |
24: | `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS` | `300000` | celld writes a Parquet file after this many milliseconds of buffered events. |
25: | `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_BYTES` | `5242880` | celld writes a Parquet file after the buffered events reach this many bytes. celld uses the limit it reaches first. |
26: | `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` | `parentbased_always_on` | A standard sampler name. `traceidratio` with `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` records a fraction of the traces. |
27: | `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | `http://localhost:4318` | The collector base URL, for the `otlp` sink. `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` also apply. |
28: | `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `celld` | The service name in the exported resource. |
29: 
30: The `bucket` sink requires the node to have a fleet bucket
31: (`CELLD_BUCKET`). The `otlp` sink works on a node without one.
32: 
33: ## What celld records
34: 
35: celld records a span for each request a stateless Worker serves, for
36: each event a cell serves (a fetch, an alarm, an RPC, a WebSocket
37: message), for each outbound `fetch()`, and for each cell start. A
38: span carries the request id, the cell, the isolate, the
39: queue wait, the outbound URL and status, and the durability facts the
40: runtime already knows.
41: 
42: celld also records each `console.log` line as a log record. The log
43: record carries the trace id and the span id of the handler that wrote
44: it, so a query can join the logs to the traces. The correlation
45: survives `await`.
46: 
47: celld reads the W3C `traceparent` header on incoming requests, so its
48: spans join the trace of the system in front of it. celld sends a
49: `traceparent` header on outbound `fetch()`, so downstream systems can
50: join too. A Worker call to a Durable Object stays in one trace.
51: 
52: The sampler decides at the start of a request. An unsampled request
53: records nothing and costs almost nothing. Under load, telemetry sheds
54: before requests do, and celld counts what it sheds.
55: 
56: celld records no metrics yet. The spans carry the durations and the
57: queue waits, so many questions a metric answers have an answer in the
58: traces, and a metrics signal can come later without a change to the
59: trace schema.
60: 
61: ## Query the bucket with DuckDB
62: 
63: ```sql
64: INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;
65: CREATE SECRET celld_telemetry (
66:   TYPE s3, KEY_ID '...', SECRET '...',
67:   ENDPOINT 's3.example.com', URL_STYLE 'path'
68: );
69: CREATE VIEW traces AS SELECT * FROM
70:   read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/*/*/*/*/*/*.parquet');
71: CREATE VIEW logs AS SELECT * FROM
72:   read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/logs/*/*/*/*/*/*.parquet');
73: 
74: -- The slowest requests.
75: SELECT name, duration_us, trace_id FROM traces
76:   ORDER BY duration_us DESC LIMIT 20;
77: 
78: -- Every log line, inside the span that wrote it.
79: SELECT l.body, t.name, t.duration_us FROM logs l
80:   JOIN traces t ON l.trace_id = t.trace_id AND l.span_id = t.span_id;
81: ```
82: 
83: An S3-compatible endpoint such as minio needs `URL_STYLE 'path'` in
84: the secret, and a plain-HTTP endpoint also needs `USE_SSL false`. AWS
85: itself does not need either.
86: 
87: The files are partitioned by node and by hour:
88: `telemetry/traces/<node>/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/<hh>/<id>.parquet`. A query
89: that reads one day therefore touches only that day's files.
90: 
91: ## File size and compaction
92: 
93: celld writes one Parquet file for each flush, on a time limit or a
94: size limit, whichever it reaches first. The defaults are 5 minutes
95: (`CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS=300000`) and 5 MB (`CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_BYTES=5242880`).
96: 
97: Keep the defaults if you run no compaction job. They make files large
98: enough for a fast query with no other moving part. A query sees an
99: event up to 5 minutes after the request, so the default suits an
100: investigation after the fact.
101: 
102: Set `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS=10000` for a near-live view, such as a
103: dashboard or an active debug session: a query then sees an event
104: within 10 seconds. A short flush makes many small files, and DuckDB
105: opens every file a query reads, so you must also run the compaction
106: job below. Turn on the compaction job first, then shorten the flush,
107: or queries grow slow within hours.
108: 
109: The `otlp` sink is the other route to a near-live view. It sends each
110: batch to a collector, so set the same short `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS`.
111: 
112: ## Compaction
113: 
114: Run a compaction job on a maintenance node, not on a celld node. celld
115: does not compact its own files, because the serving path must not do
116: storage maintenance and each node writes only the files it produced.
117: 
118: The job rewrites one past hour of small files into one large file.
119: DuckDB does the work:
120: 
121: ```sql
122: COPY (
123:   SELECT * FROM
124:     read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/<node>/2026/08/09/22/*.parquet')
125:   ORDER BY start_unix_us
126: ) TO 's3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/<node>/2026/08/09/22/compacted.parquet'
127:   (FORMAT parquet, COMPRESSION zstd);
128: ```
129: 
130: Run the job once an hour, for the hour that just ended. Do not compact
131: the current hour, because a node still writes to it. Delete the source
132: files after DuckDB writes the compacted file. The compacted file is
133: also smaller, because zstd compresses one sorted batch better than
134: many separate files.

(End of file - total 134 lines)
</content>

(`CELLD_BUCKET`). The `otlp` sink works on a node without one.

## What celld records

celld records a span for each request a stateless Worker serves, for
each event a cell serves (a fetch, an alarm, an RPC, a WebSocket
message), for each outbound `fetch()`, and for each cell start. A
span carries the request id, the cell, the isolate, the
queue wait, the outbound URL and status, and the durability facts the
runtime already knows.

celld also records each `console.log` line as a log record. The log
record carries the trace id and the span id of the handler that wrote
it, so a query can join the logs to the traces. The correlation
survives `await`.

celld reads the W3C `traceparent` header on incoming requests, so its
spans join the trace of the system in front of it. celld sends a
`traceparent` header on outbound `fetch()`, so downstream systems can
join too. A Worker call to a Durable Object stays in one trace.

The sampler decides at the start of a request. An unsampled request
records nothing and costs almost nothing. Under load, telemetry sheds
before requests do, and celld counts what it sheds.

celld records no metrics yet. The spans carry the durations and the
queue waits, so many questions a metric answers have an answer in the
traces, and a metrics signal can come later without a change to the
trace schema.

## Query the bucket with DuckDB

```sql
INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;
CREATE SECRET celld_telemetry (
  TYPE s3, KEY_ID '...', SECRET '...',
  ENDPOINT 's3.example.com', URL_STYLE 'path'
);
CREATE VIEW traces AS SELECT * FROM
  read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/*/*/*/*/*/*.parquet');
CREATE VIEW logs AS SELECT * FROM
  read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/logs/*/*/*/*/*/*.parquet');

-- The slowest requests.
SELECT name, duration_us, trace_id FROM traces
  ORDER BY duration_us DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Every log line, inside the span that wrote it.
SELECT l.body, t.name, t.duration_us FROM logs l
  JOIN traces t ON l.trace_id = t.trace_id AND l.span_id = t.span_id;
```

An S3-compatible endpoint such as minio needs `URL_STYLE 'path'` in
the secret, and a plain-HTTP endpoint also needs `USE_SSL false`. AWS
itself does not need either.

The files are partitioned by node and by hour:
`telemetry/traces/<node>/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/<hh>/<id>.parquet`. A query
that reads one day therefore touches only that day's files.

## File size and compaction

celld writes one Parquet file for each flush, on a time limit or a
size limit, whichever it reaches first. The defaults are 5 minutes
(`CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS=300000`) and 5 MB (`CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_BYTES=5242880`).

Keep the defaults if you run no compaction job. They make files large
enough for a fast query with no other moving part. A query sees an
event up to 5 minutes after the request, so the default suits an
investigation after the fact.

Set `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS=10000` for a near-live view, such as a
dashboard or an active debug session: a query then sees an event
within 10 seconds. A short flush makes many small files, and DuckDB
opens every file a query reads, so you must also run the compaction
job below. Turn on the compaction job first, then shorten the flush,
or queries grow slow within hours.

The `otlp` sink is the other route to a near-live view. It sends each
batch to a collector, so set the same short `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS`.

## Compaction

Run a compaction job on a maintenance node, not on a celld node. celld
does not compact its own files, because the serving path must not do
storage maintenance and each node writes only the files it produced.

The job rewrites one past hour of small files into one large file.
DuckDB does the work:

```sql
COPY (
  SELECT * FROM
    read_parquet('s3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/<node>/2026/08/09/22/*.parquet')
  ORDER BY start_unix_us
) TO 's3://YOUR-BUCKET/telemetry/traces/<node>/2026/08/09/22/compacted.parquet'
  (FORMAT parquet, COMPRESSION zstd);
```

Run the job once an hour, for the hour that just ended. Do not compact
the current hour, because a node still writes to it. Delete the source
files after DuckDB writes the compacted file. The compacted file is
also smaller, because zstd compresses one sorted batch better than
many separate files.

# Testing

celld makes three important promises:

- An acknowledged write is durable.
- A cell has one writer at a time. It never has two.
- Code written for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects operates the
  same on celld.

We try to break each promise at the layer where a failure shows most
clearly. We test the API contract with differential execution against the
Cloudflare runtime. We check the coordination protocol against an
exhaustively model-checked specification, and we test it with
deterministic simulation. We test the full system with fault injection
on live fleets.

## Conformance: two runtimes, one output

We test the compatibility promise differentially. We run each Workers and
Durable Objects program twice: once on workerd, the runtime binary that
Cloudflare operates in production, and once on celld, on identical bytes.
The two outputs must be equal. This shows two facts at once: the program
is real Cloudflare code, because workerd accepts it, and celld obeys the
contract, because the outputs are equal. A test cannot agree with our own
runtime by accident.

The corpus only grows. When celld gets a new API surface, we add fixtures
for that surface, and the fixtures must give equal output on the two
engines. We also port test suites from workerd itself: the Durable
Objects contract, the web-platform globals, and the upstream Web Platform
Tests. Before a release, we also replay scenarios through the full
`celld` binary in each deployment mode: storage, SQL, alarms, streams,
WebSockets, and lifecycle.

## Specification: exhaustive at small size

The coordination protocol is also specified in TLA+. Heyang Zhou wrote
the specifications against celld v0.1.0, and his model checking found
four bugs and a split-brain that lost an acknowledged write. All are
fixed. None had surfaced in our own review or testing.

Where simulation samples schedules, the checker enumerates them: at a
small configuration it visits every reachable state. The model grants
the implementation a linearizable object store and perfect shared
clocks, so a violation it finds needs no clock skew and no storage
anomaly to occur. The invariants are the first two promises at the top
of this page: one writer for each epoch, and no acknowledged write
lost. The fencing argument itself — that a stale owner's late writes
cannot cost an acknowledged write, because the epoch in the key keeps
its lineage apart — is checked, not asserted.

Every configuration carries a pinned expected verdict, and most of the
verdicts are failures: each failing configuration models a bug the
protocol once had, or a deliberately broken checker, and the model
must produce the counterexample. A configuration that stops failing
has lost its tooth. One tooth had already fallen out when the
specifications arrived; we repaired it.

Some specifications model a proposed protocol before it is built. When
the fence on write acknowledgments was redesigned, the design-stage
check produced an eight-state counterexample against the version it
replaced: a dormant cell resumes at its old epoch while its release is
in flight, acknowledges a write, and the takeover that follows
restores without it. The fix shipped; the counterexample stays as a
pinned failure.

The checker has also removed code: celld once sealed a cell's durable
history at restore, and the verdicts showed the seal defended only the
return of a write that was never acknowledged — an outcome celld does
not promise to prevent — while its permanent cut could turn a
recoverable ordering slip into a permanent loss. The seal is gone.

The specifications are a hand-synced snapshot, deliberately not in
continuous integration: a silently stale gate is worse than none. In
practice their updates have landed in the same changes that moved the
protocol, and a delta ledger records what the model does not yet
describe, including places where the model is weaker than the code
rather than wrong. Simulation remains the per-commit ratchet; the
model is its exhaustive small-configuration complement.

## Simulation: the protocol under adversarial schedules

The dangerous bugs live in the coordination: a crash during an ownership
handoff, a lease renewal that races a takeover, an alarm that fires
against a partially restored cell. These windows are nanoseconds wide and
open rarely, so a test cannot wait for them.

Thus the coordination protocol is a
[pure decision core](https://github.com/denoland/celld/tree/main/crates/logic)
with no I/O of its own: the clock, the randomness, and the object store
are interfaces, and a simulator drives the core. The simulated store
injects latency, compare-and-swap races, and lost responses; the clocks
drift apart; a node can crash at each await point. Scripted adversaries
play the cells: a handler that never returns, a write stream that stops
halfway. V8 stays out of the simulation, because V8 is not deterministic.

A seeded scheduler drives each run, so a failure is not a fluke: the seed
replays it exactly, every time, and we keep the seed until the bug is
dead. We examine each property for safety (two writers in one epoch, a
lost acknowledged write, an expired lease that comes back) and for
liveness (each armed alarm fires, and ownership settles on one node after
a crash). A property must survive tens of thousands of seeds, and the
core protocols have run through millions of different schedules.

Simulation has a known failure mode: the checker that cannot fail. So
we also test the checkers: we run deliberately broken variants of the
protocol against the properties, and the properties must find the damage.
A suite that stays green against a broken protocol is a broken suite.

## Live fleets: what simulation cannot see

Simulation cannot see the real S3 tail latency, the real kernel and
filesystem behavior, or V8 under memory pressure. The third layer is
therefore a permanent fleet lab: standard VMs from standard providers,
and a real bucket. The workloads rotate: chat rooms under many WebSocket
connections, working sets that shift across tens of thousands of cells
(each cell has a unique checksum), deployment cutovers under load, and
runs that fill the nodes to the memory limit. The lab qualifies each
release, and between releases it pushes the density and the fault
coverage further. Each run makes an archived evidence bundle: the
configuration, the verification sweeps, the node journals, the kernel
logs, and the phase timings. We keep a red run with the same care as a
green run, because a failure that the harness caught is a result, not a
retry.

We inject the faults between verification passes. A pass fetches each
cell through different nodes and compares the durable state exactly: the
status, the body, and the full message ledger. Each run therefore has a
clean picture before the fault and after it. A cell can be unavailable
for a short time while its ownership moves, but its committed state must
stay complete, and a live node must serve that state again.

The scenarios attack every seam that we know:

- Stop a node with `SIGKILL` in the middle of a write stream and delete
  its local database, so recovery can only come from the bucket. Every
  acknowledged write comes back, because the output gate held each
  response until the write was durable.
- Freeze an owner node, write to its cells through other nodes, and
  unfreeze it. The node sees that its lease moved and refuses to serve
  the old state, and each write from the other nodes lands exactly one
  time: one epoch has at most one writer.
- Cut a node off from the bucket. It fences itself, because a node that
  cannot replicate must not own cells.
- Throttle the bucket, so it answers each request with a 429. The engine
  slows to the write rate of the store and does not amplify the
  throttle, because a node that knows its replicated position does not
  ask a slow store for extra listings.
- Stop a full host at the provider level in the middle of a workload.
  Its cells move to the other nodes, and the returning host joins again
  with no duplicate residency.

Across every run of every scenario, no acknowledged write was lost and
no committed state was damaged; the verification sweeps show zero body
faults, zero status faults, and zero lost messages.

## A few numbers we trust

Each number includes the condition of its measurement. A number without
its conditions has no value.

- **The epoch fence holds under contention.** Five hundred claimants
  tried at the same time to own the same cells: 5,500 attempts, one
  writer for each epoch, zero violations.
- **A warm resident request is local.** A request to a resident cell does
  zero bucket operations and returns in p50 ~1.1 ms and p99 ~7 ms (a
  fixed-host measurement). Only a cold activation touches object storage.
- **A durable write waits for a durability proof.** A single node proves
  each write through the bucket, so one storage round trip is the minimum
  latency for that write. A fleet of two or more nodes can prove a write
  when each follower holds it on disk, and a follower fsync is much
  faster than a storage round trip: a lab fleet measured about 600 ms for
  a bucket proof and about 25 ms for a fleet proof. The bucket upload
  races every fleet proof and either one proves the write, so a slow
  follower cannot make a write slower than a bucket proof. Concurrent
  writes to one cell join one shared upload, so the throughput of one
  cell is not one round trip for each write.
- **A restore is normal work.** Placement handles the restore of an
  inactive cell as ordinary work, and not as an emergency procedure. The
  measured restore times come from the retired external replicator, so this
  page gives no number until a fleet run measures `celld-ltx`.
- **Ten small nodes held real scale.** A fleet of ten nodes, each with 4
  vCPU and 8 GB, held 10,000 resident cells and 20,000 concurrent
  WebSocket connections. We stopped two of the ten nodes, and the data of
  every cell was available again on another node in ~11 s at the tail
  (with reserve headroom).

## The failure edges we intend to find

We must also know where a policy stops, so we record the edges instead of
tuning them away. The clearest edge is the reserve headroom: a fleet that
is full to its resident limit has no space for the cells of a lost node,
so a failure of more than one node at the limit degrades the service,
and a fleet with headroom does not. We measure both sides of that line,
the good restoration with reserve and the red case without, because this
measurement is part of the work.

If you find an edge that we did not find, tell us: a schedule that breaks
a promise, a fault that we did not inject, a number that you cannot
reproduce. That is exactly the bug report that we want:
[github.com/denoland/celld/issues](https://github.com/denoland/celld/issues).

1: # Security
2: 
3: celld is an alpha. It is not safe for hostile multi-tenant use. Security fixes
4: apply to the latest release only, so older alpha builds do not receive fixes.
5: 
6: ## Security boundary
7: 
8: One fleet runs one application, and celld trusts the application code, the fleet
9: nodes, and the operators. Application code can use its configured bindings and
10: can consume shared node resources. Do not run code from mutually distrusting
11: tenants in one fleet.
12: 
13: celld depends on two external security boundaries:
14: 
15: - A trusted private network protects the internal listener. Use an encrypted
16:   overlay when the private network does not provide confidentiality.
17: - Object storage credentials control the fleet. Give each credential access to
18:   one fleet bucket only.
19: 
20: ## Separate the listeners
21: 
22: celld opens two HTTP listeners. The public listener serves the deployed Worker,
23: and the internal listener serves the peer protocol and the operator API.
24: 
25: Use `--listen` for the public listener. Expose this listener through a load
26: balancer, a reverse proxy, or a public firewall rule.
27: 
28: Use `--internal-listen` for the internal listener. Its default address is
29: `127.0.0.1:0`, so celld selects an available loopback port at each start. Use
30: `--advertise` to give peers an address that reaches this listener.
31: 
32: An explicit advertised address requires an explicit internal-listener address.
33: celld also rejects an explicit non-loopback public listener without an explicit
34: internal listener. These checks prevent an obsolete one-listener configuration.
35: 
36: celld cannot verify a hostname or a translated port. You must route the
37: advertised address to the internal listener, and you must not route it to the
38: public listener.
39: 
40: The public listener reserves only `/.well-known/celld/health`. A healthy node
41: returns a 200 response with `{"ok":true}`, and an unhealthy node returns a 503
42: response. The deployed Worker owns `/health` and every other public path.
43: 
44: The internal listener does not pass an unknown path to the Worker. It returns a
45: 404 response, so an operator request cannot become an application request.
46: 
47: ## Protect each surface
48: 
49: | Surface | Required protection |
50: | --- | --- |
51: | The public listener | Terminate TLS and authenticate users in a proxy or the application. |
52: | The internal listener | Restrict access to trusted operators and fleet nodes. Use an encrypted overlay when the private network does not provide confidentiality. |

display.text:
# Security

celld is an alpha. It is not safe for hostile multi-tenant use. Security fixes
apply to the latest release only, so older alpha builds do not receive fixes.

## Security boundary

One fleet runs one application, and celld trusts the application code, the fleet
nodes, and the operators. Application code can use its configured bindings and
can consume shared node resources. Do not run code from mutually distrusting
tenants in one fleet.

celld depends on two external security boundaries:

- A trusted private network protects the internal listener. Use an encrypted
  overlay when the private network does not provide confidentiality.
- Object storage credentials control the fleet. Give each credential access to
  one fleet bucket only.

## Separate the listeners

celld opens two HTTP listeners. The public listener serves the deployed Worker,
and the internal listener serves the peer protocol and the operator API.

Use `--listen` for the public listener. Expose this listener through a load
balancer, a reverse proxy, or a public firewall rule.

Use `--internal-listen` for the internal listener. Its default address is
`127.0.0.1:0`, so celld selects an available loopback port at each start. Use
`--advertise` to give peers an address that reaches this listener.

An explicit advertised address requires an explicit internal-listener address.
celld also rejects an explicit non-loopback public listener without an explicit
internal listener. These checks prevent an obsolete one-listener configuration.

celld cannot verify a hostname or a translated port. You must route the
advertised address to the internal listener, and you must not route it to the
public listener.

The public listener reserves only `/.well-known/celld/health`. A healthy node
returns a 200 response with `{"ok":true}`, and an unhealthy node returns a 503
response. The deployed Worker owns `/health` and every other public path.

The internal listener does not pass an unknown path to the Worker. It returns a
404 response, so an operator request cannot become an application request.

## Protect each surface

| Surface | Required protection |
| --- | --- |
| The public listener | Terminate TLS and authenticate users in a proxy or the application. |
| The internal listener | Restrict access to trusted operators and fleet nodes. Use an encrypted overlay when the private network does not provide confidentiality. |
| The fleet bucket | Restrict the credentials to one fleet bucket. |

The internal listener has three request groups:

- Most operator routes let an operator inspect or control a node without
  request authentication.
- The `/peer/tunnel` route establishes a tunnel for cell fetch, RPC, and
  WebSocket calls. The establishment request carries the fleet HMAC, a clock
  limit, and replay protection, so only a holder of the fleet secret can open
  a tunnel. Each call then crosses inside the tunnel as plain HTTP with the
  cell scope in a reserved header, and these inner calls are not signed.
- The peer-control routes coordinate fleet nodes, and the reserved-cell routes
  access runtime state. These routes use the fleet HMAC for request
  authentication, a clock limit, and replay protection.

All three groups require the trusted private network.

The tunnel permits a request body to stream to the owner, so the fleet HMAC
cannot sign an individual call. The establishment signature decides who can
open a tunnel, and a tunneled call can address an application class or a
runtime class, so every path to a runtime class demands the fleet secret.
The signature does not authenticate the bytes after the establishment, and
it does not encrypt any traffic. The private network must therefore stay
trusted, and the fleet HMAC does not replace this network boundary.

celld does not terminate TLS on either listener. Do not expose the internal
listener to the public internet. Use an encrypted overlay such as WireGuard or
Tailscale when the network does not provide the required confidentiality.

## Use the internal operator API

The internal operator API is available in the released binary. It is an alpha
interface, so a release can change its paths or response formats.

These routes do not authenticate the caller:

- `/state` reports node state.
- `/cell/<SCOPE>` resolves or activates a cell.
- `/evict/<SCOPE>` evicts a resident cell.
- `/do/<ID>` sends a direct request to an ordinary Durable Object.
- `POST /shutdown` starts a graceful ownership handoff. The
  `handoff=preserve` query prepares a same-node reload.

The `/do/<ID>` route refuses every reserved runtime class. These classes include
D1, Workflows, KV, and Queues. Their operator protocols can access application
data or change runtime state, so they use the HMAC-authenticated
`/runtime/<SCOPE>` route.

`/peer/probe` returns a signed diagnostic response. The peer protocol also
uses other reserved internal paths. An operator must not call these paths
directly.

## Set the forwarded-header policy

celld ignores `X-Forwarded-Host` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` by default. Set
`--trust-forwarded-headers` or `CELLD_TRUST_FORWARDED_HEADERS=1` only when a
trusted proxy replaces both headers. celld uses the last value in each header,
so an earlier client value does not override the proxy value.

celld always takes the path and query from the request target. It ignores the
scheme and authority in an absolute-form target, so a client cannot bypass the
host policy through the request line.

Without a trusted proxy, the `Host` header controls the hostname in
`request.url`. celld accepts a hostname, an IPv4 address, or a bracketed IPv6
address, with an optional port. It rejects malformed and noncanonical values,
and it uses `celld.local` when no source gives a valid host.

These checks keep the path and query valid, but they do not make the hostname
trustworthy. An application must not use an unchecked hostname for an
authorization decision. Use a trusted proxy or check the hostname against a
list in the Worker.

## Limit request bodies

The public Worker listener and `/do/<ID>` have a 1 GiB request body limit by
default. Set `CELLD_MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES` to a smaller positive value to
change the limit. celld returns status 413 for a declared oversized body and
when a Worker reads past the limit.

For a method other than `GET` or `HEAD`, `/do/<ID>` streams a body when its
declared length is at least 1 MiB or its length is unknown. celld collects each
smaller body before dispatch.

## Protect the fleet bucket

The fleet bucket is the root of authority for the fleet. It stores the
deployments, the cell state, the ownership leases, the node leases, and the
shared peer-authentication secret.

A person who holds the bucket credentials controls the fleet. Give each
credential access to one fleet bucket only, and replace a credential after a
suspected disclosure.

## Understand cell ownership

Each cell is a SQLite database with one writer. One node owns a cell at a time,
and an ownership epoch fences each cell. A node that loses its lease cannot
modify the current cell state.

This fencing protects storage consistency, but it does not isolate hostile
applications. See [what celld guarantees](guarantees.md) for the storage protocol,
and see [limitations](limitations.md) for the complete alpha boundary.

# Limitations

celld is an alpha. The current release has these operational limits. See
[Cloudflare compatibility](cloudflare-compat.md) for the supported services,
APIs, and Wrangler configuration.

## Fleets

- A fleet runs one application. celld has no account service, multi-tenant
  scheduler, or managed ingress.
- A fleet stores its durable state in an S3-compatible bucket, a Google Cloud
  Storage bucket, or an Azure Blob Storage container. The `celld dev` command
  instead uses a local SQLite object store. A regular node or an operator
  subcommand cannot select this local backend.
- A node does not rebalance the existing cells when it joins a fleet. Traffic
  assigns an unowned or released cell to a node with capacity.

## Networking and security

- celld does not terminate TLS. Terminate public TLS at an ingress proxy, and
  put the internal listener on a private network or an encrypted overlay.
- Peer traffic crosses the internal network as plaintext HTTP. The fleet HMAC
  authenticates tunnel establishment and control requests, and it does not
  encrypt application data on the wire. The network layer must provide the
  confidentiality.
- The fleet bucket controls the fleet. Give its credentials access to one fleet
  only. See [Security](security.md).

## Object storage credentials

- celld supports different credential methods for each object storage provider.
  See [Configure object storage](README.md#configure-object-storage) for the
  available methods and their precedence.
- Azure identity support is limited to the public Azure cloud. A managed
  identity from Azure App Service or Azure Container Apps does not work. Use a
  workload identity or a storage account key on these platforms.

## WebSockets

- An outbound Durable Object WebSocket keeps its cell resident. The connection
  closes if the cell moves to another node, so the application must store the
  connection intent and reconnect.
- A node limits the cells and outbound WebSockets that can remain resident.

## Platforms and updates

- The installer supplies binaries for Linux x86-64, Linux ARM64, and Apple
  Silicon. Windows is not supported.

display.text:
# Examples

These small Wrangler projects demonstrate progressively more of the Worker and
Durable Object surface supported by `celld`:

- `hello/` — a stateless Worker `fetch` handler
- `webapi/` — common Web Platform APIs
- `counter/` — a SQLite-backed Durable Object
- `vectordb/` — nearest-color search with a per-object `vec0` index
- `d1/` — a guestbook on a D1 database
- `r2/` — object reads, writes, and deletes on an R2 bucket
- `kv/` — key reads, writes, and deletes in a KV namespace
- `async/` — a timer and asynchronous Durable Object storage
- `body/` — request and response bodies
- `router/` — Worker-to-Durable-Object routing
- `wsecho/` — WebSocket echo with hibernation
- `wsclient/` — outbound WebSocket client from a Durable Object
- `alarm/` — a Durable Object alarm handler
- `cron/` — a cron trigger that logs each tick
- `workflow/` — a Workflow that builds a report in one durable step
- `rpc/` — Durable Object method calls through JS RPC
- `wasm/` — a Durable Object counter in Rust, compiled to Wasm with
  [workers-rs](https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-rs); needs a build step
  first (see its [README](wasm/README.md))

Deploy an example from its directory to the same bucket the nodes use:

```sh
celld deploy . --bucket s3://my-cells-bucket
```

The counter example uses the `name` query parameter as the Durable Object
name. It uses `default` when the parameter is absent. Send requests for
different names to demonstrate independent cells:

```sh
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/increment?name=alpha'
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/increment?name=beta'
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/increment?name=alpha'
```

A fleet can place the named cells on different nodes, and each cell keeps an
independent counter.

They are examples, not the complete compatibility test suite.

display.text:
# Rust library API

## Select facade

Use `celld::asyncrt::select!` when the source order must not decide a tie. The
macro selects a cyclic start for each poll, and it rejects the `biased;` token.

Use `celld::asyncrt::select_biased!` only when the source order defines the
winner of a tie. The macro polls the branches in source order. The first token
must be a non-empty string literal that states which arm wins and why.

## Durability ownership

The `celld` crate requires one `node_log::DurabilityOwner` for each local
durability stack. The owner keeps the coupled registration. It retains each
live or failed background-task handle until shutdown joins it. It also retains
each admitted release-close task and the final close handle until the
registered managed databases close.

The crate removes these public functions:

- `LtxRepl::set_shipper`
- `LtxRepl::set_bundle_sink`
- `node_log::spawn_maintenance`
- `node_log::spawn_fragment_gc`

The old setter functions installed separate strong references. A
`NodeLogManager` also retains its `LtxRepl`, so these references can create an
ownership cycle.

The old spawn functions detached their task handles. An embedding process
therefore cannot stop or join the tasks during local shutdown.

Construct a `DurabilityOwner` after the node-log recovery completes. Call
`DurabilityOwner::start_background` before the process starts its application
services, and retain the owner for the process lifetime.

Await `LtxRepl::release` when a runtime stops a cell and keeps its local files.
The method admits a managed database close to the owner task group before it
waits. Require an `Ok` result before another activation reuses the local path.
The owner retains the admitted close if the caller is cancelled. An `Err`
result retains the replica, so a later call can retry while the owner accepts
close work. The final owner shutdown also closes a retained replica.

Call `DurabilityOwner::quiesce_and_seal_within` with the remaining process time
during shutdown. A `false` result means that the local fallback ran. Therefore,
the process must not prepare a clean reload.

Stop and join all application and runtime operations before the final local
shutdown. This order prevents an activation from retaining an unregistered
database across the final shutdown snapshot.

Call `DurabilityOwner::shutdown_local_within` after an optional clean-reload
preparation. Pass the remaining process time to this method. A `false` result
means that the local fallback ran before the local shutdown completed, so the
process must exit without unwinding.

A process that has a follower store without a runtime durability stack must
use `DurabilityOwner::new_follower`. This owner starts, stops, and joins the
follower fragment collector.

pages.title: Architecture: the decision core, the effect executor, and replication
pages.purpose: Explain the clean-sheet three-tier split (celld-logic pure decision core via on_event, celld effect/adapter host, celld-ltx replication) and the single serial actor execution shape.
instructions: Establish responsibility and ownership boundaries between the crates; describe Event/Effect/State and the actor mailroom; document the deterministic-simulation seam and the __celld_domain_select macro rationale.

pages.title: Cells, scopes, and the lifecycle state machine
pages.purpose: Explain what a cell is (a named Durable Object with its own SQLite), the scope charset fence, and the full phase state machine from cold start to residency, dormancy, eviction, and takeover.

pages.title: Ownership, fencing, durability, and the output gate

pages.title: LTX replication and the in-fleet node log
pages.purpose: Explain how each committed SQLite write becomes an LTX capture and replica object, L0-L9 compaction and bundles, and the fleet node-log tier (write-all/ack-all ensemble).
instructions: Describe the LTX format surface, checkpoint/takeover capture, per-epoch prefix layout, compaction levels, tiering, and the node-log recovery takeover gate.

pages.title: The V8 JS runtime: isolates, the input gate, alarms, and WebSockets
pages.purpose: Explain how celld embeds V8 and executes Wrangler bundles: isolate pools, blockConcurrencyWhile input gating, alarms and the wake index, WebSocket hibernation, and the V8 heap limit.
instructions: Document the JS host setup, isolate pool logic, input gate semantics, alarm reconcile/wake index key scheme, and WebSocket hibernation classification.

pages.title: Deploying applications and adopting generations
pages.purpose: Explain the deployment contract: Wrangler config allowlist, manifests, deployment versions, the pointer and in-place generation adoption, cron arm, and reserved classes.

pages.title: Operating a fleet: CLI, diagnostics, and memory pressure

instructions: Cover the CLI surface, shutdown/rollout protocol, readiness gate, pressure shedding thresholds and cgroup measurement, and the fleet drain token.

pages.title: The internal operator API and /state surface

instructions: Document each operator route, the unauthenticated vs HMAC-authenticated split, and the /state fields.

pages.title: Reserved cells: D1, KV, Queues, Workflows, and cron
pages.purpose: Explain the runtime-supplied Durable Object classes that back D1 databases, KV namespaces, Queue brokers, Workflows, and cron triggers.
instructions: Focus on the reserved class naming, namespace keying, and the pure policy each backs (KV size split, queue lease generation, cron one-per-fleet arming).

pages.title: Change guides: representative maintenance tasks
pages.purpose: Focused how-to guides for safe changes: adding a Worker API surface, tuning durability/latency vars, adding a cell-backed feature, upgrading between releases.
instructions: Write practical, scoped change guides anchored to narrowest validation the repo supports.

pages.title: Security and trust model

pages.title: Telemetry: traces and logs to the bucket or OTLP

Let me map the repository structure to understand the full scope:

**Crates:**
- `crates/celld` (v0.4.0) — executable + effect adapters, `main.rs` binary, `lib.rs`
- `crates/logic` (celld-logic, v0.1.0) — pure decision core, `on_event` driven
- `crates/ltx` (celld-ltx, v0.0.0) — vendored SQLite→object-store replication (LTX format)

**Key systems discovered:**
1. Architecture: celld-logic pure decision core + celld effect executor + celld-ltx replication. Single serial Actor drives all events. `on_event` is the only way behavioral state advances.
2. Cell lifecycle: phases (residency, dormancy, cold start, takeover, shedding, eviction, activation, handoff) modeled in `crates/logic`.
3. Durability and ownership: bucket ownership records, node leases, epochs, output gate (RPO=0), fleet replication.
4. Storage: Bucket abstraction over S3/GCS/Azure with conditional writes (etags vs generations); cell scope charset fence.
5. Deployment: Wrangler deploy, manifests, generations, in-place adoption, pointer watcher.
6. Reserved cells: D1, KV, Queues, Workflows, cron — each a Durable Object class.
7. Operations: CLI (deploy, dev, diagnose, cell, d1, kv, queue), operator API, fleet readiness.
8. JS runtime: V8 isolates, input gate (blockConcurrencyWhile), websockets, alarms, wake index.
9. Memory pressure shedding & V8 heap limits.
10. Telemetry (OTEL, Parquet bucket sink, DuckDB query).
11. Testing/simulation strategy.
12. Security boundaries.
